p: Kit Darrow is a staff sergeant in the Missouri Air National Guard. She's the crew chief on a KC-135 tanker the shop calls two two eight, after the last three numbers on its tail.
A crew chief keeps one jet ready to fly and signs for it. Kit is also qualified to run the engines on the ground, with the jet chocked and going nowhere.
She's thirty two. Her drill weekends are at Tolliver Field, a Guard base that shares a runway with the town airport in Tolliver, a river town on the Missouri about two hours from Kansas City.
The rest of the month she works rotating shifts at the town's water treatment plant. Her husband, Graham, teaches physics and chemistry at Tolliver High.
The test in this book is the AFOQT, the Air Force Officer Qualifying Test. Most people headed for an Air Force commission have to sit it.
It opens at ten past four on a Saturday morning in January 2027, on the first drill weekend of the year.
The people you'll hear from first.
Lonnie Fisk. Airman first class, twenty, Kit's assistant crew chief. He works overnights at a distribution center too.
Arlen Boyd. Master sergeant and flight chief. He trained Kit, and his name was on her jet before hers.
Kemp. A staff sergeant who crews the jet parked next to Kit's.
Vern Pruett. A retired navigator. His is the voice you'll hear after each of Kit's calls, saying what he'd have told her.
Graham Darrow. Kit's husband. They've been married nine years.
At 4:10 on a Saturday morning in January, Kit Darrow sat in the left seat of a jet that wasn't allowed to go anywhere.

Two two eight was chocked front and back, brake set, throttles up at run power, and every rivet in her was shoving at chocks that weren't going anywhere either. Kit could feel it in her fillings. Out front the north ramp at Tolliver Field was black and wet. The Guard hangars were lit up orange, and past them was the Missouri River, which at that hour you mostly knew was there because it was darker than everything else. Eight degrees outside. The heater was losing.

Night shift had changed a fuel pump on number three, and this run was the leak check. It was on the schedule at four so it would be done before the morning launch, and before half of Tolliver woke up and called the airport about the noise. Fisk was out by the nose on a long headset cord, watching for leaks, a reflective vest and a flashlight and not much else.
Three's dry, Sergeant. No leaks. I looked twice.

She pulled the throttles back. The jet settled onto its gear like a kid who'd been told no. She ran the shutdown checklist, then stayed put after the last engine quit, listening to the gyros wind down and the metal tick.

Engine run qualified meant she could start the engines, run them, check them, and shut them down. It didn't mean she could let off the brakes. In eleven years on the flight line this was the only seat she'd ever had up front: the left one, in a jet that was chocked. Her name was stenciled under the pilot's window outside, CREW CHIEF SSGT K. DARROW, white block letters Boyd had painted in 2018 over the place where his own name had been.

Behind the pilots, where the navigator used to sit, there was nothing now but a row of bolt holes in the floor. She'd sat in a seat like that once, at seven, on a family day, in one of the wing's jets. Which jet, she couldn't have told you. A man's voice. His hand pointing up at the ceiling, and her staring hard at the spot, trying to see what he saw. Wanting something so badly she'd cried in the car on the way home.

At 4:50 she walked into the shop. Somebody had made the coffee too strong, which was the only way the shop made coffee, and on the corkboard next to the pot, pinned over a notice about a lost pair of gloves, was a new sheet of paper.

Pilot vacancy, summer 2027 hiring board. The wing will select one applicant for undergraduate pilot training. The selection board convenes Saturday, July 10, 2027. Applicants must hold a bachelor's degree, meet commissioning standards, and have AFOQT scores on file by June 1, 2027. Minimum scores are on page two. Applicants must not have reached their 33rd birthday by the board date. Selection is contingent on a flight physical and on final approval above the wing.

She read it twice. Then she read the birthday line a third time, pulled a blank work card out of the binder rack and did the math on the back of it, the math she'd known she would do before she got to it. June 3, thirty three. July 10, the board. Five weeks. Next summer she'd be a whole year further past it.
Five weeks over a line somebody had typed. She folded the card in half, put it in her chest pocket, and couldn't have said yet whether five weeks was a wall or a crack.

Seven years ago she'd put in for a board like this one, and that winter she'd pulled her package to stay for the spring inspection, because Boyd had asked her to. That was the story. She'd told it so many times it had worn smooth, like a wrench handle.
Vern's Nav Table: what you're sitting down to.

Vern Pruett, lieutenant colonel, retired. One Sunday in January a crew chief named Kit Darrow took the stool next to mine at the Riverside Diner. I'll get to that. Until I do, whenever she makes a call, you'll hear what I'd have told her.
Most break room talk about this test is wrong. Here are the plain facts.

It's the Air Force Officer Qualifying Test, the AFOQT. The current version is Form T, in use since 2014. You take it on a computer at a Pearson test center, a base test office, or an ROTC detachment, and you need a voucher from a recruiter or a base test control officer to book it. It's free, and it isn't given at MEPS. Plan on about five hours with breaks.

There are twelve subtests, and eleven of them count. The current Pearson page lists them in this order, with items and minutes. Verbal Analogies, 25 in 8. Arithmetic Reasoning, 25 in 29. Word Knowledge, 25 in 5. Math Knowledge, 25 in 22. Reading Comprehension, 25 in 24. Situational Judgment, 16 in 35. A fifteen minute break. The Self-Description Inventory, 240 statements in 45 minutes, which isn't scored. Physical Science, 20 in 10. Table Reading, 40 in 7. Instrument Comprehension, 25 in 5. Block Counting, 30 in 5. Aviation Information, 20 in 8.

One of those needs a word now, because it's where people spend themselves. The Self-Description Inventory is 240 statements about how you work and deal with people, in 45 minutes. That's a little over eleven seconds each. It isn't graded, so there's no score to win. Its answers help match people to Air Force jobs.

You can lose your legs in there, though. Every statement gets a mark on a five step agree scale, from strongly disagree up to strongly agree, and 240 of them is a lot of marks. Five scored subtests come right after it, and the tables and the instrument pictures want a fresh eye. Take the first honest answer, keep a steady pace, and don't go back over the ones you've done. Come out of those 45 minutes with something left. We'll get to the rest of it later.

Every item has five choices except Instrument Comprehension, which has four. Your score is the number you get right. Nothing comes off for a wrong answer, so never leave one blank. Scores post in two to three business days.
This course isn't affiliated with or endorsed by the Department of the Air Force, AFPC, or Pearson.

How the exam asks it. The 2015 paper pamphlet lists different numbers for a few subtests, including 50 Situational Judgment picks. The Pearson page is newer, so this course uses its numbers. Check it again before your date.

Subtest scores roll into composites, each a percentile from 1 to 99. A 60 means you beat about sixty percent of the people it's measured against. Verbal comes from Verbal Analogies, Word Knowledge and Reading Comprehension. Quantitative comes from Arithmetic Reasoning and Math Knowledge. Academic Aptitude uses all five. Pilot leans on Math Knowledge, Table Reading, Instrument Comprehension and Aviation Information. Situational Judgment is reported on its own. Two more rated composites matter if you'd take a seat other than the left one. CSO, for combat systems officers, the job navigators grew into, was Word Knowledge, Math Knowledge, Table Reading and Block Counting in the 2015 pamphlet. ABM, for air battle managers, was Verbal Analogies, Math Knowledge, Table Reading, Instrument Comprehension, Block Counting and Aviation Information. Newer citations list a different mix for both, so treat those two lists as the old ones and check the current version with your unit.

Any commission needs at least Verbal 15 and Quantitative 10. A pilot applicant needs Pilot 25. Some Guard units have also asked pilot applicants for a CSO score of at least 10, with Pilot plus CSO adding up to 50 or more. Ask your own unit or recruiter what they use. Your board's announcement may set a PCSM minimum too.

PCSM is the pilot candidate selection method. It combines your Pilot composite, a separate computer test called the TBAS, and your logged flying hours into a score from 1 to 99. The formula isn't published, and since the end of 2021 credit for flying hours stops at 41.

You get two attempts, at least 90 days apart, and a third takes a waiver. Scores are superscored, so your best result on each composite across your attempts is the one that counts, and Form T scores don't expire. A second try can only raise your best number.

How the exam asks it. If you keep one composite in your head, keep Pilot: Math Knowledge, Table Reading, Instrument Comprehension and Aviation Information. Those are the four to push if you want a cockpit.
Situational Judgment, and why the story works the way it does.

Each Situational Judgment item gives you a problem a junior officer might face and five things you could do about it. You pick the most effective and the least effective. The key comes from experienced officers, and it rewards what works with people, not just what's allowed.

Handle it directly, privately, and at the lowest level first. Talk to the person before you talk about them. Use the chain of command after a direct try fails, not in place of one. Don't go over a head, don't brief the boss behind a peer's back, and don't quietly do somebody's work for them. Stay honest when it's awkward.

One exception matters. If something false is still in motion, like a bad record headed for a jet or a commander, you stop it and report it now. The rule was never "never escalate." It's "escalate in the right order."

When this story asks what Kit should say to somebody, that's this subtest in disguise. Six competencies sit under it: Integrity and Professionalism, Leadership, Resource Management, Communication, Innovation, and Mentoring.

How the exam asks it. For most effective, look for the option that deals with the person directly and in private. For least effective, look for public correction, going over a head, ignoring the problem, or a lie.

Verbal Analogies give you a pair and ask you to finish a second pair that matches it. Say the first pair as a sentence. A navigator measures with a sextant. Then try each answer in that same sentence. Most analogies use a short list of relationships: part to whole, tool to user, worker to workplace, degree, like warm to hot, cause and effect, opposites, synonyms, and type to category.

Word Knowledge gives you one word and five choices, and you pick the closest meaning. Twenty five words in five minutes is twelve seconds a word. Break it into pieces. Bene is good, mal is bad, chron is time, spec is look.
How the exam asks it. Watch for an answer that fits the topic but not the relationship. Navigator and crew chief are both aviation words. That doesn't make every aviation word right.
The jet from outside: parts and axes.

The fuselage is the body. The wings make lift, with ailerons on the trailing edges for roll and flaps that add lift and drag for takeoff and landing. The tail is the empennage: a vertical stabilizer with the rudder hinged to it, and a horizontal stabilizer with the elevator.

An airplane turns around three axes that cross at the center of gravity. The longitudinal axis runs nose to tail. Turning around it is roll, and the ailerons do it. The lateral axis runs wingtip to wingtip. That's pitch, and the elevator does it. The vertical axis runs top to bottom. That's yaw, and the rudder does it. Pull back on the yoke, and the elevator's trailing edge goes up, the tail goes down, and the nose comes up. Turn the yoke left, and the left aileron goes up while the right one goes down.

Airport beacons too. White and green alternating is a lighted land airport. White and yellow is a water airport. Green, yellow and white is a heliport. A military field alternates white and green, with the white in two quick flashes.
How the exam asks it. Know each control with its axis and its motion: ailerons, longitudinal, roll. Elevator, lateral, pitch. Rudder, vertical, yaw.

Table Reading gives you a big grid with X values across the top and Y values down the side, zero in the middle and negatives on one side. Each item names an X and a Y and asks for the number where they cross. Many of the wrong choices are the cells next door, so the whole skill is not slipping a row. Accuracy first, then speed.

The clock on it is 40 items in 7 minutes, about 10 seconds each, and that's what makes it a perceptual speed test. Nobody's checking whether you can read a chart. Everybody can. It's checking whether you can do it forty times running and never let your eye slide a line. A miss here isn't a hard item. It's an easy one you read wrong, and that's a point you had.

Here's how I'd work one. Say it asks for X minus 2 and Y plus 1. Put a finger on the minus 2 column along the top and a finger from your other hand on the plus 1 row down the side, then slide them together. Read the number under your fingers before you look at the five choices, and then go find it. Look at the choices first and a number from the cell next door will seem familiar, and familiar feels like right. At the nav table I held a pencil flat under the row of a fuel chart on bumpy nights. Same trick, older equipment.

Pace comes from rhythm, not hurry. Halfway through the seven minutes you want to be near item twenty. If you're behind, don't rush the reading. Spend less time staring at the choices. And when the clock's about to run out, put an answer on everything that's left.

Arithmetic Reasoning is word problems, 25 in 29 minutes, with scratch paper. Nobody's told me for certain whether a calculator's allowed, so practice without one. A lot of them are rates. Amount equals rate times time, so time is the amount divided by the rate. Nine thousand pounds at fifteen hundred a minute is six minutes.
How the exam asks it. On Table Reading, X is the column across the top and Y is the row down the side. Swapping them is the most expensive mistake on the page.

Fisk came in behind her with his ears red from the cold and stood at her shoulder, reading. He was twenty, her assistant crew chief since August, and he'd come straight off the overnight at the distribution center out on Route 9. She knew that because he still had the scanner lanyard around his neck.
Pilot slot. Huh. He leaned in. 'Selection is contingent on a flight physical.' So is that like a maybe? Does the physical come before you get picked, or after?
A. Tell him it means the physical can be waived for strong applicants.
B. Tell him it means the physical happens on the same day as the board.
C. Tell him it means you get picked first and take the physical later.
D. Tell him it means the selection depends on passing the physical.

It depends on it. You can get picked, and if you fail the physical, you're unpicked. Fisk nodded slowly. So it's a maybe. It's a yes with a string on it. He liked that. He said it twice under his breath on the way out to the truck.

That'll hold, Sergeant. Contingent means dependent on. Something that's contingent on something else only holds if the other thing happens. The test likes words like this because people half know them. Concurrent means at the same time, and it sounds close enough to trip you at twelve seconds a word.
At 5:40 the expediter came on the radio. The receivers on the morning's refueling track had changed overnight, and planning wanted twelve thousand more pounds of fuel on two two eight.

The truck was already parked at the wingtip. Hooking up would take about six minutes. It pushed fuel at about fifteen hundred pounds a minute, and closing out and disconnecting took five more. The expediter wanted one number, and Kit worked it in her head like a chlorine feed rate at the water plant at three in the morning, before anybody could offer her a calculator.
How long should Kit tell the expediter the whole fuel job will take?
A. Tell the expediter 8 minutes, start of hookup to disconnect.
B. Tell the expediter 25 minutes, with some padding built in.
C. Tell the expediter 14 minutes, start of hookup to disconnect.
D. Tell the expediter 19 minutes, start of hookup to disconnect.
Nineteen minutes. Six to hook up, eight pumping, five to close out. A pause on the radio. Copy nineteen. It took twenty one, because the nozzle stuck, and nobody held that against her.

Right. Log it. Break it into legs and add them. Twelve thousand pounds at fifteen hundred a minute is twelve thousand divided by fifteen hundred, which is eight minutes. Six plus eight plus five is nineteen. Arithmetic Reasoning is mostly this: a rate, a couple of fixed times, and one leg that's easy to forget.

The engines were turning by 6:25 when the aircraft commander came on the interphone. Crew chief, pilot. We're showing low quantity on one of the hydraulic systems. Pressure's normal. Can you take a look?

Kit needed the fault isolation table out of the forms binder and a light to read it by. She knelt at her toolbox on the ramp and opened the lid. Inside was the shadow board, gray foam with a cutout for every tool she owned, and the cutout for her big flashlight was empty. Under the foam, where she never looked, were a few sheets of paper folded small, the creases gone soft from being folded so long.

Fisk had borrowed the flashlight for the leak check at four. She'd watched him take it. He was twenty feet off at the nose on the headset cord, hands jammed in his vest, rocking heel to toe to keep his feet awake.
Kit needs that flashlight now, and a tool can't stay missing near a jet. What should she do?
A. Borrow a flashlight from the crew and sort it out after the launch.
B. Walk over to Fisk and ask him quietly if he still has the flashlight.
C. Call a tool hunt on the radio and hold the launch until it turns up.
D. Ask Fisk over the interphone, with the crew listening, where it went.

She walks over and stands close enough that nobody on the headset can hear her over the engines. Fisk. My light. His hand goes to his vest and comes back with it. Sleepy to sick in about a second, she'd swear later. Sergeant, I forgot I had it. I know. We'll talk after. Right now I need it. The outline in the foam is full again before the interphone asks a second time.

That's the fix I'd have taken. Integrity and Professionalism, and Communication. You knew who had it, so the fastest fix was also the most private one: ask the person, face to face. If he hadn't had it, you'd stop the launch and run a tool hunt, and that would be right too. The key leans the same way on the test. Lowest level first, then go wider if that fails.

She read the table on her knee with the flashlight in her teeth and the forms binder open on the toolbox lid. It was the cold weather page for exactly what the crew had: quantity low, pressure normal. The rows went down the side by the reading on the reservoir gauge. The columns went across the top by outside air temperature. Every cell held the number of the step to go to.
The fault isolation table, cold weather page. Rows by the reservoir reading, columns by outside air temperature, and a step number in every cell.
The gauge on the reservoir read 2.0. The thermometer bolted to the hangar wall read 8 degrees.
Kit has the gauge reading and the temperature. How should she pull the right step out of the table?
A. Go with step 22, the one she remembers from a cold morning last winter.
B. Put a finger on the 2.0 row and one on the 0 to 15 column.
C. Read the crew the whole page and let the pilots choose a step.
D. Count the columns over from the left edge, then read down to the cell.

Left finger on 2.0, right finger on 0 to 15, slide until they touch. Step 23. She checks the cells around it, 22 to the right and 32 above, so she knows what a slip would have cost: a reservoir topped off cold, puking fluid on the ramp by noon. Pilot, crew chief. Quantity's normal for the temperature. Step 23, no servicing. It'll come up as it warms. Copy. Thanks, Chief.

That'll hold, Sergeant. Table Reading is this, forty times in seven minutes. Find the row, find the column, read where they cross. The wrong answers on the test are the neighbors, one row up or one column over, because that's the slip people actually make. Two fingers beat one eye.

At 7:02 she stood off the left wingtip in the dark and saluted. The aircraft commander saluted back through the side window, and two two eight rolled. Kit and Fisk stood at the edge of the ramp while it swung onto the runway and the engines went from loud to a lot louder.

It took most of the runway. Tankers full of gas always did, and Kit always held her breath for the last thousand feet anyway, which Boyd said was a waste of a good breath. Past the Bravo turnoff the nose came up, then the mains, and then it was a red light blinking out over the river toward Kansas.
I know it's the elevator, Sergeant. I watch it move on every ops check. What I can't keep straight is which way it goes when they pull back.
Which way should Kit tell Fisk the elevator moves when the pilot pulls back?
A. Tell him the elevator's trailing edge comes up, so the tail goes down.
B. Tell him one half of the elevator goes up and the other goes down.
C. Tell him the pilot pulls back on the yoke, and the nose follows.
D. Tell him the elevator's trailing edge drops, and that lifts the nose.

Trailing edge comes up. The wind leans on it and shoves the tail down. Tail down, nose up. Same as a seesaw at the park, only this one weighs close to three hundred thousand pounds. Fisk tried it with his hand, wrist down, fingers up, and looked at it like it had told him a secret. That's pitch. Ailerons are roll, rudder's yaw. I'll quiz you Sunday.

Right. Log it. Pitch is the jet turning on its lateral axis. Picture a broom handle pushed through her from wingtip to wingtip, and the elevator's what twists it. I got this backwards myself at twenty two, in a classroom at Mather with the radiator banging. Pull back and the elevator's trailing edge goes up, not down. Aviation Information will ask you more than once and dress it differently every time.

By 7:06 it was in the clouds, and the ramp went quiet enough to hear the generator cart. Fisk hadn't moved. Both hands in his vest, chin down, like an airman who'd been thinking about a flashlight for a while.

He'd been bracing for this since the flashlight came out of his pocket in front of her. He'd come straight off a ten hour shift. At four in the morning he'd taken a tool out of her box without signing for it, and then forgotten it was on him.
The jet's gone and the ramp is quiet. How should Kit deal with Fisk about the flashlight?
A. Let it go this once, and tell him not to worry about it.
B. Tell Boyd that Fisk took a tool without signing, and let him handle it.
C. Use it at the shift huddle as a tool control lesson, with no names.
D. Take Fisk aside now and talk through the sign out with him.

Walk with me. They go around the side of the truck, out of the wind. She asks what happened and lets him tell all of it: the warehouse, the ten hours, the leak check at four, the light in his pocket. Then she says, You sign for it every time, even from my box, even at four. If you're too tired to remember a flashlight, I need to know before you're under a jet. He nods for a while. Yes, Sergeant. And eat something.

That's the fix I'd have taken. Leadership and Mentoring. Private, soon, and specific: what happened, what you expect, what you need to hear from him. You found the cause, which is fatigue and not carelessness, and the cause is the part that comes back. The key rewards this order every time. Talk to the person first. The chain is for when that doesn't work.
Boyd found her at the corkboard at eleven, holding a coffee she'd let go cold, reading the posting for the fourth time.

Master Sergeant Arlen Boyd had been on the KC-135 since 1996 and on her since she was twenty one. He'd taught her to safety wire, to read a forms binder, to tell a pilot no. He was fifty one. When the wing converted to the KC-46 around 2030 he'd retire, and he'd told her more than once that the shop would be hers after him, the way some men tell their kids about the house.

He looked at the paper, and then at her, and something crossed his face that she knew. It was the look he got every time a board posting went up, a man paying on a debt he thought was his. She'd let him carry it ever since. You're not thinking about that, he said. Are you?
A. Tell him the wing needs pilots who know the jet from the outside.
B. Tell him no, she's just reading it, and get back to work.
C. Tell him yes, she is, and that he'll hear it from her first.
D. Ask him why he wants to know, and put the question back on him.

Yeah. I'm thinking about it. Whatever I decide, you'll hear it from me first. Boyd looks at the paper a long time. Okay, he says. Okay. Seven years ago I asked you to stay. I know. He nods once, goes back to his office, and shuts the door, which he never does.

That'll hold, Sergeant. Communication, with some integrity in it. He asked a direct question, so he gets a direct answer, in private, from you. Telling him he'll hear it from you first is what the key rewards with a peer or a boss: nobody should find out from a corkboard. You didn't have to explain yourself yet. You just couldn't lie.
At 4:30 the jet was back, written up and put to bed with covers on and chocks in, and the shop was emptying out. Kit stood in front of the corkboard in her coat.

The posting was two pages stapled together, and she hadn't lifted the first one until now. The second page was the minimum scores and the packet instructions: who signed, in what order, due when. At the bottom, in smaller type, it said that routing begins with the applicant's immediate supervisor. That was Boyd.
It was the only copy on the board. The hallway was empty.
The posting is the only one on the board, and nobody's around. What should Kit do with it?
A. Leave it up, and get her own copy at the orderly room.
B. Leave it up, and walk out without taking any of it.
C. Leave it up, and take a photo of the first page on her phone.
D. Take it down, fold it up, and put it in her coat pocket.

The orderly room is closing, and the staff sergeant at the desk prints both pages without asking why. She folds them in thirds and puts them in her coat. The board copy stays where it is, over the lost gloves, for whoever else wants it.

Right. Log it. Integrity and Professionalism, in a small room. That paper belongs to everybody in the wing who might want it, and your own copy cost you a walk down the hall. Read all of it, too. You almost didn't lift the first page, and the second page is the one that says who signs.

Sunday morning it was nine degrees, and the break room smelled like popcorn somebody had burned on night shift. Kemp, the crew chief on the jet parked next to two two eight, had the posting off the corkboard and was reading it out loud to four people.

Don't bother, anybody. The colonel sent Corbin Haas from avionics two years ago because everybody liked him, and he washed out. She's never doing that again. Whoever she picks, it'll be some kid out of the university with a pilot's license and a rich uncle.
Somebody laughed. Kemp looked over at Kit, and then at the folded paper in her coat pocket, and grinned.
Kemp is running down Corbin and the colonel in front of the shop. How should Kit handle it?
A. Laugh along with the room and say she's only curious.
B. Catch Kemp alone after the huddle and ask him to drop it.
C. Tell the room that Corbin's washout is his business, not theirs.
D. Pin a note under the posting that Corbin's record is nobody's business.

She doesn't say anything in the room. After the huddle she finds Kemp at his toolbox. Corbin's in the avionics shop every drill. He can hear that story from anybody. He doesn't need to hear it from us. Kemp shrugs, but he isn't grinning anymore. Yeah. Okay. Fair. It doesn't come up again.

That's the fix I'd have taken. Communication, and a little Leadership without the stripes. A peer who says something unfair in public gets a private word, not a public one. You stood up for a man who wasn't in the room, and you didn't make Kemp defend himself in front of four people, which is the only way he'd have dug in.

The Riverside Diner sat on the county road a mile outside the main gate, a chrome box with a counter, eight booths and a lot full of pickups. Kit took the last stool at five thirty, still in her flight line coat, bringing the cold in with her.

The man on the next stool was seventy something and sat up straighter than she did. Corduroy jacket. Pencil behind his ear. A crossword folded down to one square of clues. He looked at her coat, and at the red remove before flight streamer on her zipper with 228 inked on it in marker. Then at the folded paper in her pocket, where the top line showed: PILOT VACANCY.

I navigated her. Twenty one years, on and off. Vern Pruett. He held out a hand. It was a strong hand with a class ring worn thin on one side. Retired. I keep the heritage room on base now, Saturdays, for the eleven people a year who come in.

Family day came up into her throat and stuck there. Back then the wing had a whole ramp of tankers with a navigator in every one, and asking a stranger at a lunch counter if he remembered one little girl from one family day felt too much like asking for something. She shook his hand instead.

Out the window the airport beacon turned over the field, green, then white, green, then white. Vern tipped his head at it. You've seen that a thousand times, Sergeant. Coming in at night, what does it tell a pilot about this field?
A. That it's a heliport, with pads in place of a runway.
B. That it's a military airfield, for the Guard base on the north side.
C. That it's a lighted land airport, open at night.
D. That it's a water airport, set up for seaplanes on the river.

Lighted land airport. Green and white. Good. Not a teacher's good. More like a man ticking a line off a checklist he'd run a few hundred times. Plenty of folks from the base say military. The military beacons do the white twice, real quick, between the greens. He watched the beacon go around again. This is a civilian field you all borrow.

That'll hold, Sergeant. How many colors did you count? Two. Green, then white, over and over, is an airport on land that's lit for night. Learn four patterns and these are free points. White and yellow is for seaplanes. Green, yellow and white is a heliport. Base people miss the military one, because it's green and white too. The difference is the white. It comes twice, fast, like somebody blinking.

He asked about the posting, so she told him. He'd taken a much older version of the test himself in 1973, he said, on paper, in a gym that smelled like floor wax. He took the pencil from behind his ear, a yellow number two sharpened with a pocketknife, and pulled a napkin out of the holder to go with it.

The first eight minutes are analogies. Twenty five of them. People think it's vocabulary. It's relationships. He printed in square block capitals that nobody would ever need to read twice: SEXTANT IS TO NAVIGATOR AS BLANK IS TO CREW CHIEF.
Make a sentence out of the first pair. Then the same sentence with the second. Go on.
Which word fills Vern's blank, so both pairs share the same relationship?
A. Write TORQUE WRENCH in the blank.
B. Write AIRCRAFT in the blank.
C. Write FLIGHT LINE in the blank.
D. Write HEADSET in the blank.

A navigator measures with a sextant. A crew chief measures with a torque wrench. She wrote it under his capitals, smaller. Vern looked at it for a long time, for something that simple. That's the sentence, he said. Most people write airplane and can't tell me why.

Right. Log it. What does a sextant do? Measures. So what does a crew chief measure with? You had it before I finished asking. Verbal Analogies is a relationship test. Say the first pair as a sentence, a navigator measures with a sextant, and the second pair has to fit the same sentence. Name the relationship and the wrong answers fall away.
Vern folded the napkin once and slid it over to her. Then he went back to his crossword and filled in a word, and she understood that he wasn't going to offer.

She'd never asked anybody for anything that was only for her. She'd asked Boyd for training, for the shop. She'd asked the plant for nights so the drill weekends would work. She'd asked Graham to wait, more than once. After the degree. After the inspection. Every time she'd told him what it was for, and every time he'd said okay.
The waitress brought the check. Vern put a five on it for his coffee and reached for his coat.
Vern is putting on his coat, and he hasn't offered anything. What should Kit do?
A. Thank him for the napkin and let him go home.
B. Ask if he'd come teach the young airmen in her shop.
C. Ask him if he'd sit down and teach her the test.
D. Tell him she'll stop by the heritage room sometime.

Would you teach me? For the test. It came out in the wrong order, and she let it. Vern stopped with one arm in his coat and looked at her the way he'd looked at the napkin. Tuesday, he said. Nineteen hundred. Cedar Street, the brick ranch with the dead hedge. Bring a pencil, Sergeant. I'm not lending you mine.

That's the fix I'd have taken. Mentoring runs both ways, and it starts with somebody asking. You went to the one man at that counter who could help, and you asked for the actual thing. I'd have said yes to a clear ask from anybody. A dressed up one I'd have had to guess at, and I was too old for guessing.

Graham had the kitchen warm and the radio on low, a basketball game nobody was winning. He was at the fridge whiteboard with a marker, moving her plant shifts around his lab nights for the week, same as every Sunday. In the corner of Saturday he'd drawn his little cartoon tanker. He always did on drill weekends.
She set Vern's napkin on the counter by the mail. Then the posting, flattened out with the side of her hand.

Graham read it standing up, the way he read lab reports, all the way to the end. He got to the birthday and she watched him do the same math she had. He taught physics. He was faster at it than she was.
Most of the weekend had gone right, and she could feel it in her shoulders, the good kind of tired.

She had an answer ready. She'd had it ready since the corkboard: the wing needed pilots who knew the jet, the board would want somebody local, it would be good for the shop. All of it was true. She'd been saying it to herself all weekend so it would be there when she needed it.
She didn't say any of it.
She'd never said it out loud before. It came out smaller than she meant it to, about the size it had been at seven, in the back of her mother's car on the way home from family day.
Graham looked at her. The game went to a commercial. He didn't answer right away. She noticed, and she'd go on noticing it for weeks.

He capped the marker without writing anything. Then he hugged her, hard, the marker still in his hand, and over his shoulder she could see the whole week on the fridge, every block of it, and the little tanker in the corner of Saturday.
